newsitem.title: UK: PMI survey shows stg reducing price pressures.
newsitem.headline: PMI survey shows stg reducing price pressures.

text.p: The relentless rise in sterling helped keep a lid on price pressures in the UK manufacturing sector in November, adding weight to Chancellor Kenneth Clarke's bid to keep interest rates on hold at least until the new year.
The November purchasing managers (PMI) survey showed manufacturing growing for the sixth consecutive month but price pressures remaining subdued.
"The strength of sterling appears to have brought to a halt the upwards trend in the...index," said General Accident economist Andrew Milligan.
"Together with good news on inflation components, this will be useful support for the Chancellor in his battle to limit the tightening of monetary policy in the run up to the election."
The Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply (CIPS) said the PMI index dipped to 54.4 pct in November from October's 54.5. A reading above 50.0 indicates manufacturing is expanding.
The prices index fell to 42.3 percent in November from 44.1 percent in October as over a fifth of companies saw prices fall.
The CIPS said although prices of some goods bought in the UK continued to harden as demand picked up, sterling's rise reduced the prices paid for many imported materials.
"The one important thing in the survey is the rise in sterling," said Union Discount economist Philip Uglow.

"It's helping to keep prices down at the moment and has also caused a reduction in order books...We're only seeing the real beginning of it now, it'll be a long term effect. As long as these gains are maintained at these levels, sterling will have a dampening effect over the next year or so."
Sterling rose by around 10 percent between August and November on a trade weighted basis, leaving input prices falling for the thirteenth month in a row in November.
Economists said Clarke would use the survey evidence to counter calls from Bank of England governor Eddie George for a rise in interest rates at their next monetary policy meeting on December 11.

"There's a risk the Chancellor will miss the RPIX target, but if he does it will not be by a great deal...and he may be prepared to tough it out at next week's meeting (and leave rates on hold)," said BankAmerica economist Jeremy Hawkins.
Uglow said Clarke would use the PMI data to question the Bank's view that sterling's rise would not noticeably dampen inflation.

"But the real question is whether that's enough to warrant no further hikes in interest rates. If the Chancellor is serious about hitting his 2.5 percent inflation target, he will need to tighten monetary policy," he said.
Uglow added he expected rates to rise by a quarter point in December from their present 6.0 percent, and then remain on hold until after the election, which must held by May next year.

Money supply figures released on Monday showed M0 rose by 0.9 percent in November, giving a 7.5 percent annual rate, unchanged from October but still well-above the government's zero to four percent monitoring range.

"M0 is not a very accurate indicator of month-on-month changes in retail sales. But this points tentatively to a slight rise in the level of high street activity in November," said HSBC economist Dharshini David.
Economists said the CBI distributive trades survey on Thursday would give a more concrete indication of the strength of pre-Christmas retail sales.
